title: Design Video Streaming
subtitle: Follow one uploaded video through transcoding and segmenting, then watch a player pull it from a CDN and adapt to bandwidth.
learn: Why uploads go straight to object storage and are processed asynchronously
How a transcoding pipeline turns one source file into a ladder of renditions
How HLS and DASH split video into short segments listed in a manifest
How a player switches quality mid-stream without the server being involved
Why the CDN carries almost all the bytes and the metadata service carries almost none

steps.title: One file in, thousands of ways out
steps.body: A creator uploads one 10-minute 1080p video file. Viewers will watch it on a phone over weak mobile data, on a laptop with fast fibre, and on a TV, all at the same time, from every continent. No single file or server fits all of them. This lesson builds the system that turns one upload into something every viewer can play smoothly. It has two halves: a slow, heavy "prepare the video" path and a huge, cheap "deliver the video" path.
steps.idea: Streaming is two problems: a slow, heavy write path (upload and process) and a huge, cheap read path (deliver bytes).
steps.caption: One source video, many different viewers.

steps.title: Upload straight to storage
steps.body: The creator app asks the upload service to start. The service checks who is uploading and creates a video record marked "processing". It returns a presigned URL: a temporary signed link that lets the app write straight into object storage. The app then sends the file (about 600 MB here) in chunks of roughly 8 MB, and can resume if the connection drops. The big bytes never pass through our app servers.
steps.idea: Presigned, chunked, resumable uploads keep large files off your app servers and survive flaky networks.
steps.caption: A record is created, then chunks flow straight into the raw video store.

steps.title: Queue the work
steps.body: When the last chunk lands, the upload is marked complete and a job message goes onto a queue (a waiting line for tasks). Transcoding (re-encoding the video) takes minutes, so the creator is not kept waiting. Workers pull jobs when they have capacity, and a failed job is simply retried. A long video is split into pieces a few seconds long, so many workers can encode different pieces in parallel.
steps.idea: A queue decouples slow processing from the upload request and lets you scale workers by backlog.
steps.caption: A job is queued and a worker picks it up.

steps.title: Encode a bitrate ladder
steps.body: Workers read the source and re-encode it several times. The result is a bitrate ladder: the same video at several qualities, for example 240p at 0.4 Mbps, 360p at 0.8, 480p at 1.4, 720p at 3 and 1080p at 5 Mbps. Together that is about 10.6 Mbps, so a 10-minute video becomes roughly 800 MB across all versions (renditions). This is CPU-heavy work, often done on GPUs or dedicated encoder chips. Audio is encoded once or twice and shared.
steps.idea: Each rendition is a separate encode of the same content at a different resolution and bitrate.
steps.caption: Workers read the raw file and produce 5 renditions of it.

steps.title: Cut into short segments
steps.body: Each rendition is cut into segments of about 4 seconds, saved as ordinary files, and listed in order in a playlist. The two main formats are HLS (Apple's, .m3u8 playlists) and DASH (an open standard, .mpd manifests); both can share the same segment files (CMAF). Every segment starts on a keyframe (a full picture that needs no earlier frames), and the cut points are identical in every rendition. A 600-second video gives 150 segments per rendition, so about 750 files.
steps.idea: Segments are plain static files, so any HTTP server or CDN can serve them. Aligned cuts make switching quality safe.
steps.caption: Segments and playlists land in the segment store.

steps.title: Mark it ready
steps.body: When every rendition is done, a worker updates the metadata service: the status becomes "ready" and the record stores the playlist location, the duration, the available renditions and thumbnails. The metadata service holds titles, owners, permissions and counters, usually in a database with a cache in front. It stores kilobytes per video, never the video itself. Search and recommendations read from it too.
steps.idea: Metadata is small and queried constantly; media is huge and fetched by URL. Keep them in separate systems.
steps.caption: The video record flips from processing to ready.

steps.title: Player asks what to play
steps.body: A viewer opens the video. The player asks the metadata service, which checks the viewer may watch it and returns the title plus a signed playlist URL. The player then downloads the master playlist from the CDN (a network of cache servers near viewers). It is a small file listing every rendition. No video bytes have moved yet, and the metadata service is now out of the picture for the rest of the session.
steps.idea: The metadata call happens once per video; everything after it is plain file fetching.
steps.caption: Metadata returns a playlist URL, and the player fetches the master playlist.

steps.title: Segments come from the edge
steps.body: The player requests the first segment at a middle quality. The request goes to the nearest CDN edge. On the first view the edge does not have it, so it fetches the segment from the segment store (a cache miss) and keeps a copy. Every later viewer in that region gets it straight from the edge. Segments never change, so they can be cached for a very long time. Startup takes about 1.2 seconds.
steps.idea: Only the first viewer per region pays the trip to the origin; the CDN serves everyone after that.
steps.caption: Cache miss: the edge fetches from the origin, keeps a copy, and serves it.

steps.title: Bandwidth drops, quality follows
steps.body: The player times each segment download and watches how much video it has buffered. When a train enters a tunnel, speed drops and the buffer shrinks, so the player asks for the next segment at 360p instead of 480p. This is adaptive bitrate. The server does nothing special; it serves whichever file is requested. Because every rendition is cut at the same points, the switch is invisible apart from softer pixels. Popular segments are now cached, so the edge hit rate climbs.
steps.idea: Adaptive bitrate is decided by the player, using ordinary file requests. This keeps the servers stateless and cacheable.
steps.caption: The player drops to 360p, and the edge serves it from cache.

steps.title: Heavy write, cheap read
steps.body: Upload goes straight to storage, a queue feeds workers that encode the ladder and cut segments, and the metadata service records when the video is ready. Playback is one metadata call, then segment files from a CDN, with the player choosing the quality. The write path is slow and compute-heavy but runs once per video. The read path runs millions of times, so it is built from cacheable static files.
steps.idea: Do the expensive work once, ahead of time, so serving is just fetching cached files.
steps.caption: The whole path, from upload to playback.

quiz.q: Why does the creator app send file chunks directly to object storage with a presigned URL instead of through the upload service?
options: Object storage encrypts data and the upload service cannot
Presigned URLs make the upload faster by using a better protocol
Large file bytes would otherwise tie up app servers and bandwidth, while the service still controls who may upload
The upload service cannot accept files over 1 MB
quiz.why: The upload service only authorizes and records the upload. Moving gigabytes through it would waste its capacity, and object storage already handles large, resumable writes well.

quiz.q: Segments for every rendition are cut at the same timestamps, each starting on a keyframe. What does that make possible?
options: The CDN can merge renditions into one file
The player can switch quality at a segment boundary without a glitch
Transcoding runs without needing a queue
The metadata service can skip storing the manifest URL
quiz.why: A segment that begins on a keyframe can be decoded on its own. Aligned boundaries mean segment 40 at 360p picks up exactly where segment 39 at 480p ended.

quiz.q: A video goes viral and 2 million people start watching within an hour. Which part of the design protects the origin segment store?
options: The transcode queue absorbs the viewers
More transcoding workers are added automatically
Segments are immutable static files, so CDN edges cache them and serve nearly every request
quiz.why: Each segment is fetched from the origin about once per region, then served from cache. Viewers hitting the edge never touch the origin.

quiz.q: A 2-hour movie takes 6 hours to transcode on one machine. What is the most effective fix within this design?
options: Split the source into chunks of a few seconds and encode them in parallel on many workers
Encode only one rendition and let the player upscale
Store the source in a faster database
Have the CDN transcode on the first request
quiz.why: Video chunks can be encoded independently, so parallelism cuts wall-clock time almost linearly. The segment playlist already treats the output as separate files, so no heavy re-joining is needed.

cheatsheet.def: The set of renditions of one video, from low resolution and bitrate to high, e.g. 240p at 0.4 Mbps up to 1080p at 5 Mbps.
Decoding a video and re-encoding it at a different resolution, bitrate, or codec. CPU/GPU heavy, so run it asynchronously on workers.
A short file (about 2 to 6 seconds) of one rendition. Starts on a keyframe so it decodes independently.
Two adaptive streaming standards that deliver video as segments listed in a playlist or manifest (.m3u8 / .mpd) over plain HTTP.
The player picks the next segment's rendition from measured throughput and buffer level. The server stays unaware.
A time-limited signed link that lets a client read or write one object in storage without holding credentials.
Origin holds the full set of segments. Edges cache the popular ones near viewers; only misses travel back to origin.
Delay from pressing play to the first picture. Driven by the metadata call, manifest fetch, and first segment download.

lab.prompt: Design the video platform for 5 million daily active viewers watching an average of 40 minutes each, with 50,000 new uploads per day averaging 8 minutes. Sketch the upload path, the processing pipeline, the delivery path, and estimate storage and peak egress.
requirements: Uploads must be resumable and must not pass large files through the application servers.
Each video is playable at several quality levels and adapts to changing bandwidth.
Playback starts within about 2 seconds for most viewers worldwide.
A failed or slow transcode must not lose the upload or block other videos.
Estimate daily new storage for all renditions and peak delivery bandwidth, stating your assumptions.
hints: Use a ladder of about 10 Mbps total. 8 minutes is 480 s, so one video is roughly 600 MB across renditions. Multiply by 50,000 uploads.
Watch time: 5 million viewers times 40 minutes. Convert to bytes using an average delivered bitrate of about 3 Mbps, then think about peak versus average (a rule of thumb is 2 to 3 times).
Ask which pieces are idempotent. Re-running a transcode job for the same video should overwrite the same output paths.
Decide where the metadata lives and what the playback request returns. Keep its size and cost far below the media path.
Consider long-tail content: most videos get few views, so edge caches hold the popular head while the tail comes from origin.
checklist: Presigned, chunked upload direct to object storage, with a record created in processing state.
Queue plus parallel transcode workers, with retries and a dead-letter path for bad files.
Multiple renditions cut into aligned segments with HLS or DASH manifests.
Metadata service separate from media storage, returning a signed manifest URL.
CDN in front of the segment store, with long TTLs for immutable segments.
Back-of-envelope numbers for storage per day and peak egress, with assumptions written down.
